extracted.intended_audience: educated readers / natural philosophers (late 17th–early 18th century); general readers interested in natural theology and anatomy
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length explanatory treatment (natural-philosophy style) of respiration, properties of air, experimental demonstrations (bellows, air‑pump, syringe), and the anatomy and circulation of the blood, argued toward design/theological conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many muscles involved in breathing (including the midriff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Now if you add to these the Midriff, being the principal Instrument of them all ... there must, according to this Computation, be at least a hundred Muscles made use of in one single Action of Breathing as strongly as we can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Van Horne and Acta Lipsiensia; emphasizes complexity and many differently oriented muscle fibres as evidence of design. Used to argue that such disposition is not produced by chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midriff (diaphragm) as principal instrument of respiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Midriff, being the principal Instrument of them all, and which, according to the Opinion of that great Anatomist Verleyen, consists of two, or it may be three Muscles more ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The midriff's action (pressing down / moving) is compared to the pump/sucker and is central to enlarging the thoracic cavity and producing air inflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air's elastic (expansive) property (vis elastica) causes inflow during chest expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: the Air ... has in it, among other Properties, an Expansive Power (Vis Elastica) ... as soon as the Breast is enlarged by the Operation of the above-mentioned Muscles, this Air immediately rushes into the Wind-pipe and Lungs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The elastic force of external air is taken as the immediate mechanical cause of air entering the lungs when the thorax enlarges; author promises fuller treatment of air itself later and experimental proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of respiration with a pair of bellows
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove this by a Comparison, one need only represent to one's self a Pair of Bellows ... nothing more is requisite in order to draw the Air into the Mouth A, or Tube AB, than to separate the sides ED and FG from each other; by which Means the Space ED GF is enlarged; and so the Air that was contained therein being weakened ... the external air ... does by its Elastic Force crowd itself into the mouth of the Bellows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of bellows as an accessible analogy: enlargement of cavity weakens internal air so stronger external air flows in. Explicit mapping: Tube AB = wind-pipe; cavity ED GF = thorax; bellows-sucker = midriff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-pump experiment with lungs to demonstrate mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the Covering OP be laid upon the pump ... at the Extremity of the little Tube AN there is another screwed on at BC, the End of which is stuck into the Wind-pipe of a little Piece of Lungs D, which is tied fast to it. ... when the Piston ... is thrust ... one sees that the Piece of Lungs D hangs in the Space E ... but the little Cock at N being turned, the Sucker is drawn backwards ... the Space that contained the included Air is much larger ... the external Air rushing to the Piece of Lungs D through the Tube AB, fills it up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed procedural description: attach lung to pump, operate piston and cocks, observe expansion/contraction correlating with pump action. Author points out analogy to thorax/midriff and that the air-pump reproduces the same effect mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syringe experiment showing non-elastic matter won't fill newly-made empty spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: if an empty Space be made in the Syringe AB, by drawing up the Sucker FA ... the Water in the little Glass DE ... will by no means rise up into the Tube, nor fill the empty Space in the Syringe ... because the Water DE has no sensible Elasticity or Spring in itself
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that only elastic fluids (like air) will rush to fill an enlarged cavity; water (non-elastic in this sense) will not, so presence of elastic property in ambient medium is required for respiration to occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with glass vial and water to visualize air rushing into lungs
rubrics_metrics.description: take a little glass Vial ... tie it to the Tube BC ... thrust the End of the Tube as far as it can into the Water, then shut the Cock ... enlarge the Space as before ... open the little Cock N, and he will see that the External Air ... will put the Water into a very violent Motion, just as if one should set his Mouth to the other End of the Tube ... and blow through the Water as hard as he can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple demonstration available to observers without dissected lungs to show the action of external air entering an enlarged cavity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy: thorax and midriff correspond to air-pump cavity and sucker
rubrics_metrics.description: if you will suppose the Tube AB to be the Wind-pipe, the Space PRI to be the Cavity of the Thorax, and the Sucker LM the Midriff, there will be a mighty analogy between that Experiment and the Business of Respiration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author repeatedly builds the mechanical analogy to reinforce the explanatory model: muscular thoracic expansion creates weakened internal air and external elastic air rushes in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of elasticity in medium for breathing to occur
rubrics_metrics.description: although there be Space enough prepared in the Breast, in order for Breathing, yet, in many Cases no Air (if, like the Water, it should happen not to be Elastic, nor heavy enough) would come in
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that mere enlargement of cavity is not sufficient — the surrounding medium must have elastic (spring) properties to flow in; experimental support via syringe/water example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of respiration (hypothesized): cooling blood / aiding air passage / imparting nitrous spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: the most learned Naturalists are not entirely agreed, whether it serves to cool the Blood, or, whether it be to procure a more convenient Passage for the Air alone through the little Tubes of the Lungs, and thereby to produce a better Mixture of Blood; or lastly, to communicate a Nitrous Spirit to the same in the Lungs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes competing hypotheses and mentions experiments (e.g., dark venous blood turning bright red after exposure to air or to saltpeter solutions) without committing fully; leaves disputes to later ages but confines himself to experimental inquiry of which effects are true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrupted air causes pestilential diseases; air as common vector
rubrics_metrics.description: these kinds of Diseases must proceed from one common Source ... and that can be nothing else but the Air, which is common to all Mankind. ... exposing a Bucket of Water a whole Night to the Air ... there stood a kind of a Cream or Scum of divers Colours ... given a Dog to drink, the Poison was so strong, that he died of it in a few Hours
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation (Leiden plague example) used to argue that air-borne corruption can poison even familiar atmospheres; used in moral/theological persuasion about providence and preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air deposits particles in the blood (leaves something behind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Opinion, that the Air being drawn into the Lungs, leaves something there (whatever it may be) and does not come out again of the same Temper, seems to be somewhat probable from certain Experiments ... it should appear credible, that the Air leaves behind it in the Lungs the same Particles which serve to maintain Flame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites experiments and Homberg's observation (scent of turpentine leading to scented urine) to suggest inhaled particles enter the blood; presented cautiously as probable, not settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arterial distribution: the aorta branches to supply all body parts
rubrics_metrics.description: we know, that there is not any one Part of the Body as yet discovered, in which we find that the Blood is not conveyed thither by the Branches of this great Artery ... be it for Nourishment or Motion, and likewise for the Separation of other Humours and farther Uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive anatomical description follows (carotids, subclavians, celiac, mesenteric, renal, spermatic, iliacs, etc.) to show purposeful distribution; references to plates/figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venous return: veins carry blood back to the heart corresponding to arterial branches
rubrics_metrics.description: the same Blood is to be found, to which there is not again a Vein. Which Branch carries that Blood back to the Heart, that was brought from thence by the Artery, to all the other Parts. ... observe how these Veins run along the Body, and after having performed their Office, carry the Blood back to the Heart
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anatomical mapping (figs cited) showing venous channels (jugulars, vertebrals, vena cava ascendens, subclavian veins) as necessary returns; used to explain a circulation loop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive narrowing of arteries toward periphery ensures adequate distribution and produces the pulse
rubrics_metrics.description: Can it be imagined ... that the Arteries are larger next the Heart, and gradually narrower, and divided into numerous little Branches, as they go farther from it? The Reason of which is, to prevent the Blood, which issues with so much Violence out of the Heart, from passing by the Lateral Branches, and following its way only in the large Vessels; ... it presses every way upon the Sides of the Artery, and expanding the same (which is the Cause of the Pulse) rushes into the Lateral or Side-Branches
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explains functional morphology: tapering and branching regulate flow, ensuring peripheral tissues receive their share; offers this as evidence of contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative estimate of blood circulation frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Left Ventricle of the Heart may contain about two Ounces of Blood ... if we suppose each Pulse is made in a Second of an Hour ... this will produce 3600 Pulses every Hour ... This together will make the Quantity of 600 Pounds of Blood ... that will pass through the Heart in an Hour. ... the whole Blood passes through the Heart 24 times in an Hour; that is to say, 576 times in a Day and a Night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step-by-step numerical argument using assumed ventricular volume, pulse rate, and total blood volume (citations of Harvey, Lower, Lister) to show rapid and repeated circulation; alternative pulse-rate assumptions discussed to show robustness of conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and orientation of vascular orifices and branches indicate purposeful design
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissect a Vein or an Artery lengthwise, and observe how regularly the Orifices in both of them lie; through which, from the latter, the Blood passes into the Branches that spring out of it, and by the former is received into the Vein out of the Branches thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author invites readers to inspect anatomical figures (Lower, plates) and dissection observations to perceive the purposive arrangement, offered as philosophical/theological evidence rather than mere mechanical accident.
